newsitem.title: ALBANIA: European aid experts meet Albanian prime minister.
newsitem.headline: European aid experts meet Albanian prime minister.

text.p: European relief experts met Albanian leaders on Thursday to discuss a proposed foreign security force for protecting humanitarian aid to help pull the troubled Balkan nation back from anarchy.

A six-year-old boy hit when gunmen sprayed bullets at a bus near Tirana on Wednesday died overnight from his wounds, bringing the death toll to two. Six other people were hurt in one of the most violent incidents near the capital.

Prime Minister Bashkim Fino was holding talks with a 15-strong European delegation headed by Dutch diplomat Jan de Marchant et d'Ansembourg, on a second trip to the former communist nation in two weeks.

The two sides hope to work out ways to ensure that emergency relief gets through, including the possible use of a foreign security force favoured by six European Union nations who have sent military advisers to Albania.
Fino said the immediate problems were restoring public order and reorganising Albania's police force after a wave of violence in which more than 100 people have died.
The moves were "to settle the problem of different criminal gangs, disturbing the government and the common people as well", he told the Albanian Daily News in an interview published on Thursday.
Much of the south of Europe's poorest nation remains in the hands of rival armed rival gangs, rebels without a cause except for their demand that rightwing President Sali Berisha resign.
D'Ansembourg's team, expected to stay several days, will also debate Albania's plans for elections in June and ways of bolstering democracy for the country's 3.4 million people.
The six EU nations who have sent military experts to Albania to investigate the possibility of a security force to protect aid have failed to secure an international green light for their plan.

The 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), the continent's top security body, failed to approve a mandate for a military mission at talks in Vienna on Wednesday. "The meeting ended in disarray," one diplomat said.

It was unclear when the OSCE would meet again and the six EU states -- France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Austria and Greece -- may now get bogged down in seeking authority from the United Nations or could take the riskier step of going in alone.

Non-EU members Turkey and Romania have also expressed willingness to take part. But acting solely on Tirana's invitation could expose them to charges of propping up Berisha if they got drawn into any shooting.

Fino has said that any foreign forces would be very small in number and would help keep open the ports of Vlore and Durres and protect Tirana's international airport, which reopened for normal business this week.
D'Ansembourg, also said any relief mission would "not involve thousands of troops... It will depend on how many (personnel) the Albanians themselves can offer", he said.
D'Ansembourg's team includes experts from the OSCE, the 15-nation European Union and its executive Commission and the 40-nation Council of Europe.
Finance Minister Arben Malaj said that Albania's problems went far beyond emergency assistance. The EU estimates that the country needs $10 million of medical supplies and 10,000 tonnes of flour.
"The emergency aid is not a solution to our problem," he told Albanian television. "It may just push the country for a while, but may prepare a harder future for us."
In Brussels, the European Commission said on Wednesday it had agreed to send two million Ecus ($2.3 million) worth of humanitarian aid to victims of the crisis.
